MEASURED 2026-08-22 while building `incomplete_published_contract`. THE FIRST CUT OF THE DETECTOR WAS GREEN OVER EXACTLY THE THING IT EXISTS TO CHECK, and the cause was a schema default.

Five of the nine interface agreement axes are enums DEFAULTING to `unspecified` (`medium`, `paradigm`, `payload_format`, `auth`, `transport_security`). The store MATERIALISES defaults on write (`Schema::validate_node`), so every Interface ever created already carries the word. A presence test — is this property set? — therefore counts `unspecified` as an ANSWER.

MEASURED BEFORE THE FIX, on reflow2's own three published boundaries:
  `ifc:mcp-tools-http`   read 9 of 9 COMPLETE while its `medium` said `unspecified`
  `ifc:graph-export`     reported 4 unset axes where there are 6
  `ifc:mcp-tools`        9 of 9, and this one is genuinely true

⭐ SO A COMPLETENESS CHECK OVER DEFAULTED FIELDS MEASURES NOTHING, AND REPORTS SUCCESS. It is not that the check was slightly wrong; it is that the property it tested was guaranteed true for every node in every design. The fix reads `unspecified` as UNSET.

⚠️ AND THE OPPOSITE ERROR IS JUST AS AVAILABLE: `none` IS AN ANSWER. `auth: none` and `transport_security: none` on an unauthenticated local pipe are deliberate statements, and `ifc:mcp-tools` makes exactly them. Sweeping `none` in with `unspecified` would nag a design that had answered honestly. DECLARED ABSENCE AND UNDECLARED ABSENCE ARE DIFFERENT FACTS, and only a vocabulary that separates them can tell a finished contract from an untouched one.

🛑 THIS IS THE THIRD TIME IN ONE DAY THAT MATERIALISED DEFAULTS DECIDED A DESIGN. (1) `vocabulary_coverage` can never name a DEFAULTED property as unused, so what it reports is the undefaulted optional only — an under-count, stated as an honest limit. (2) `no_published_boundary` had to exist at all because `Interface.designation` defaults to `internal`, making "unclassified" and "deliberately internal" indistinguishable, while `Artifact.audience` needs no such companion BECAUSE it is undefaulted. (3) This.

THE GENERAL FORM, and it is the argument `req:defaults-do-not-assert` was accepted on, now with a mechanism rather than a principle: A STORED DEFAULT DOES NOT MERELY ASSERT SOMETHING NOBODY SAID — IT MAKES THE ABSENCE UNDETECTABLE. Every later computation that tries to find out whether anyone answered gets `true`, and no test written against the schema alone can see it, because the schema is where the lie is. The three cases above differ in what they cost: an under-count, an extra detector, and a check that could not fail.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT SAY: that defaults are wrong. `Requirement.status` defaulting to `proposed` is right, because `proposed` is a true statement about a requirement nobody has ruled on. The distinction is whether the default is a FACT about the unset state or a GUESS standing in for one — and `unspecified` is the rare case of a default that honestly names its own emptiness, which is why the repair here was cheap. The expensive ones are defaults that name a plausible value.
